opening_arguments.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

I stand for the proposition that **Islam promotes peace**—not as a slogan, but as a central principle rooted in its scripture, ethics, law, and prophetic teaching.

The very language of Islam points to peace. The word *Islam* is connected to submission to God, and the word *salaam* means peace. The everyday greeting of Muslims across the world is: **“As-salaamu ‘alaykum” — “Peace be upon you.”** That is not incidental; it reflects an ideal: that a Muslim’s presence should bring safety, dignity, and mercy to others.

The Qur’an teaches that human life is sacred. It declares:

> “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely.”  
> — **Qur’an 5:32**

That is one of the strongest moral statements about the value of human life found in any religious text. Islam does not treat violence lightly; it treats the taking of life as a grave moral catastrophe.

Islam also explicitly rejects forced religion:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:256**

A faith that commands “no compulsion” cannot honestly be described as a religion whose essence is coercion. Islam’s vision of society is not one where people are forced into belief, but one where faith is sincere, conscience is respected, and human beings are accountable before God.

The Qur’an commands Muslims to live justly even with those they dislike:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> — **Qur’an 5:8**

This is a profound peace-building principle. Many conflicts arise because people excuse injustice when it is directed at their enemies. Islam forbids that. Justice is not optional; it is a religious duty, even toward opponents.

The Qur’an also encourages peaceful relations with those who do not fight Muslims:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who do not fight you because of religion or drive you from your homes. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.”  
> — **Qur’an 60:8**

And when peace is offered, Muslims are commanded to accept it:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and put your trust in God.”  
> — **Qur’an 8:61**

So the Qur’anic principle is clear: peace is preferred, justice is required, and violence is limited to situations of aggression and persecution—not expansionism or cruelty.

The Prophet Muhammad’s teachings reinforce this. He said:

> “A Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40**

That statement defines Muslim character through safety: people should be safe from a Muslim’s speech and actions. He also taught:

> “You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not truly believe until you love one another. Shall I tell you something which, if you do it, will cause you to love one another? Spread peace among yourselves.”  
> — **Sahih Muslim 54**

The Prophet also prohibited the killing of non-combatants in war. Reports in both Bukhari and Muslim record that he condemned the killing of women and children.  
— **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**

This matters because Islam is not naïve about conflict. It recognizes that aggression, oppression, and self-defense exist. But even when fighting is permitted, it is morally restricted. Islam does not glorify violence; it regulates and restrains it.

At its core, Islam promotes a peace built on four pillars: **mercy, justice, sanctity of life, and reconciliation**. The Qur’an describes the Prophet Muhammad as:

> “A mercy to the worlds.”  
> — **Qur’an 21:107**

And it commands:

> “Indeed, God commands justice, excellence, and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression.”  
> — **Qur’an 16:90**

That is the moral architecture of peace.

Of course, some people have committed violence in the name of Islam, just as people have committed violence in the name of many religions, ideologies, and nations. But the misuse of a tradition does not define the tradition. The question is not whether every Muslim has always lived up to Islam’s teachings; no community can claim that. The question is what Islam itself promotes. And its foundational texts repeatedly call for peace, mercy, justice, restraint, forgiveness, and the protection of innocent life.

Therefore, I affirm: **Islam promotes peace—not passive peace at any price, but principled peace rooted in justice, human dignity, and accountability before God.**
opening_arguments.against:
**Opening argument against the proposition “Islam promotes peace”**

Ladies and gentlemen, I oppose the proposition not because I deny that many Muslims are peaceful, compassionate people, or that Islamic scripture contains verses about mercy, forgiveness, and restraint. It does. My argument is narrower and more precise: the claim that **Islam, as a religious system, promotes peace** is too broad and cannot be sustained when we examine its foundational texts, traditional law, and historical application.

A religion that truly promotes peace should consistently protect freedom of conscience, reject religious coercion, and limit violence to genuine self-defense. Yet Islamic sources contain not only peaceful passages, but also explicit commands and precedents for armed struggle, subordination of non-Muslims, and punishment of apostasy.

For example, the Qur’an commands believers to fight certain non-Muslim groups: “Fight those who do not believe in Allah… among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya with willing submission and feel themselves subdued” (Qur’an 9:29). That is not merely self-defense; it describes a political order in which non-Muslims may live only under Muslim dominance and taxation. Another verse says, “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is wholly for Allah” (Qur’an 8:39; cf. 2:193). Qur’an 9:5, often called the “Sword Verse,” says to “kill the polytheists wherever you find them” after the sacred months, though interpretations differ on its historical scope. Even if some argue these verses are contextual, they have undeniably been used by classical jurists and later movements as legal and moral support for religious warfare.

The Hadith literature reinforces the problem. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Muhammad is reported to have said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…” (Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22). Another hadith states: “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” (Sahih al-Bukhari 3017). A tradition that treats apostasy as a capital offense cannot be described, without qualification, as promoting peace in the modern sense of freedom, tolerance, and non-coercion.

This is not merely theoretical. Classical Islamic jurisprudence developed doctrines of **jihad**, **dhimma**, and **jizya** that placed non-Muslims in a subordinate legal category. Scholars of Islamic law such as Majid Khadduri and Rudolph Peters have documented that jihad in classical law was not only an inner spiritual struggle but also a legal doctrine of armed conflict for the expansion or defense of Muslim rule. That does not mean every Muslim endorsed violence, but it does mean violence and coercive hierarchy are not alien distortions imposed from outside Islam; they are part of the tradition’s legal and scriptural inheritance.

The proposition may respond by citing verses such as “There is no compulsion in religion” (Qur’an 2:256) or “If they incline to peace, then incline to it” (Qur’an 8:61). Those verses matter, and they explain why many Muslims sincerely build peaceful lives and communities. But the presence of peaceful verses does not erase the presence of militant and coercive ones. The real question is not whether Islam contains some teachings compatible with peace. It plainly does. The question is whether Islam, taken as a whole, **promotes peace**. The evidence shows a mixed and contested tradition—one that has promoted charity and mercy in some contexts, but also religious war, unequal status for non-Muslims, and punishment for dissent in others.

Therefore, the proposition is too simplistic. A more accurate statement would be: **many Muslims promote peace, and Islamic sources can be interpreted peacefully.** But Islam as a total doctrinal, legal, and historical system does not consistently promote peace. For that reason, the motion should be rejected.

**Citations**

- Qur’an 2:193; 8:39; 8:61; 9:5; 9:29; 47:4.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22 — “I have been commanded to fight the people…”  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 3017 — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1955.  
- Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, Markus Wiener, 1996.  
- Michael Bonner, *Jihad in Islamic History: Doctrines and Practice*, Princeton University Press, 2006.

round_1.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

My opponent’s argument is thoughtful, but it rests on a mistaken assumption: that for Islam to “promote peace,” it must be absolute pacifism and must contain no rules for war, punishment, or political order. That is not how any serious legal or religious tradition works. Islam emerged in a world of tribal warfare, persecution, empire, and political violence. Its question was not, “Can conflict ever exist?” but rather: **How do we restrain conflict, protect life, forbid aggression, preserve conscience, and make peace the preferred outcome?**

When the Islamic sources are read as a whole, the answer is clear: Islam promotes peace through justice, mercy, restraint, and reconciliation.

---

## 1. The “fighting verses” are contextual, not a blanket command to attack non-Muslims

My opponent cited Qur’an 9:5, often called the “Sword Verse”:

> “Kill the polytheists wherever you find them…”  
> — Qur’an 9:5

But quoting that phrase alone removes the surrounding context. The same passage begins by discussing **treaty-breaking tribes**, not all non-Muslims for all time. Immediately before it, the Qur’an says:

> “Except for those polytheists with whom you made a treaty and who have not failed you in anything or supported anyone against you; so complete their treaty until their term.”  
> — Qur’an 9:4

And shortly after, the Qur’an says:

> “If any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of God, then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> — Qur’an 9:6

That is crucial. If Qur’an 9:5 were a universal order to kill all polytheists, Qur’an 9:6 would make no sense. The same passage commands Muslims to protect an enemy non-Muslim who seeks safety and escort him securely away. That is not indiscriminate violence; that is a wartime rule of restraint.

The context is made even clearer later:

> “Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, intended to expel the Messenger, and attacked you first?”  
> — Qur’an 9:13

So the issue is not peaceful religious difference. The issue is aggression, treaty violation, and war.

This is consistent with the Qur’an’s general rule:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

That verse establishes the principle: fighting is permitted against aggression, but transgression is forbidden.

---

## 2. “Fight until there is no fitnah” refers to ending persecution, not forcing conversion

My opponent cited:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for God.”  
> — Qur’an 2:193; 8:39

But *fitnah* in this context refers to persecution, oppression, and the violent suppression of religious freedom. The early Muslims were expelled, tortured, boycotted, and attacked because of their faith. The verse is not saying, “Fight until everyone becomes Muslim.” In fact, the very same passage says:

> “If they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors.”  
> — Qur’an 2:193

And Qur’an 8:38 says:

> “Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has previously occurred will be forgiven for them.”  
> — Qur’an 8:38

So the command is not endless war. It is: resist persecution, stop aggression, and if the enemy stops, hostilities stop.

This is also supported by:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and put your trust in God.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

A scripture that commands acceptance of peace when peace is offered cannot be honestly reduced to a doctrine of permanent war.

---

## 3. Qur’an 9:29 and jizya do not prove forced religion

My opponent also cited Qur’an 9:29:

> “Fight those who do not believe in God… among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya…”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

This verse is often presented as if it commands forced conversion. But it does not say, “Fight them until they become Muslim.” It says that conflict ends when a political tax is paid. Whatever one thinks of pre-modern taxation systems, the verse itself recognizes the continued existence of Jews and Christians under Muslim rule. That is not forced conversion.

Historically, *jizya* functioned as a tax on non-Muslim adult males in exchange for protection and exemption from Muslim military obligations, while Muslims paid *zakat* and were subject to military duties. One may argue that this was not modern liberal equality, but the debate topic is whether Islam promotes peace, not whether seventh-century political arrangements match twenty-first-century citizenship models.

More importantly, the Qur’an gives a general principle for peaceful coexistence with non-Muslims:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who do not fight you because of religion or drive you from your homes. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

That verse is broad, explicit, and moral: kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims are not merely allowed; they are loved by God.

---

## 4. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” must be read with the Qur’an and Prophetic practice

My opponent cited the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22

But Islamic interpretation does not read one hadith in isolation while ignoring the Qur’an, other hadith, and the Prophet’s own conduct. If this hadith meant “fight every non-Muslim until conversion,” it would contradict:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

It would also contradict the Prophet’s treaties with non-Muslims, including the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, and the Qur’an’s command to protect polytheists who seek safety:

> “Grant him protection… then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> — Qur’an 9:6

It would also contradict Qur’an 9:29 itself, which allows Jews and Christians to remain non-Muslim under Muslim governance.

Therefore, the hadith is best understood in its historical setting: the Prophet was speaking about hostile forces in Arabia who were actively resisting the Muslim community, not issuing a universal command to wage war on every non-Muslim individual.

The Prophet’s broader teaching was peace-oriented. He said:

> “Do not wish to meet the enemy; ask God for safety. But if you meet them, be patient.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 2966; Sahih Muslim 1742

That is not glorification of war. It is reluctance toward war and preference for safety.

He also said:

> “A Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40

This defines Muslim character by the safety one provides to others.

---

## 5. Apostasy: the Qur’an does not prescribe a worldly death penalty for mere belief change

My opponent cited:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3017

This is a serious text, and it deserves serious treatment. But again, it must be read with the Qur’an and the wider legal context.

The Qur’an mentions apostasy multiple times but does not prescribe a worldly death penalty for simply changing one’s belief. For example:

> “Whoever among you turns back from his religion and dies as a disbeliever — for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter…”  
> — Qur’an 2:217

The punishment mentioned is spiritual and eschatological, not a worldly execution.

Another verse says:

> “Indeed, those who believe, then disbelieve, then believe, then disbelieve, then increase in disbelief — God will not forgive them…”  
> — Qur’an 4:137

This verse describes people moving in and out of belief more than once. That would be impossible if the Qur’an required immediate execution for mere apostasy.

The Qur’an also says:

> “The truth is from your Lord; so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.”  
> — Qur’an 18:29

And:

> “Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed. Would you then compel people until they become believers?”  
> — Qur’an 10:99

So how did many jurists understand the hadith? In the pre-modern context, apostasy was often tied to political treason, rebellion, or joining enemy forces during wartime. This is supported by another hadith that gives the category more fully:

> “It is not lawful to shed the blood of a Muslim except in three cases… one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676

The phrase “separates from the community” is important. It suggests not a private change of conscience, but a public act of rebellion or treason against the community.

So even if classical jurists often adopted harsh rulings, the Qur’anic foundation is clear: belief cannot be forced, and mere inward disbelief is not met with a Qur’anic worldly punishment.

---

## 6. Classical Islamic law included war doctrines, but also strong restraints on war

My opponent mentions classical doctrines of jihad, dhimma, and jizya. It is true that classical Islamic law developed rules for warfare and governance. But having a law of war does not mean a religion promotes violence. In fact, rules of war often exist to limit violence.

Islamic sources prohibit treachery, mutilation, and the killing of non-combatants. The Prophet condemned the killing of women and children:

> “A woman was found killed in one of the battles, and the Messenger of God condemned the killing of women and children.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744

The Qur’an also gives the earliest permission to fight in explicitly defensive terms:

> “Permission to fight has been given to those who are fought because they have been wronged…”  
> — Qur’an 22:39

And the next verse says that if aggression were not resisted:

> “Monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques, in which God’s name is much mentioned, would have been destroyed.”  
> — Qur’an 22:40

This is remarkable. The Qur’an justifies defensive struggle not only to protect mosques, but also monasteries, churches, and synagogues. That is a peace-building principle: religious communities must be protected from violent persecution.

---

## 7. Islam promotes peace, but not passive surrender to injustice

The opposition seems to define peace as the absence of any sanctioned force. But Islam’s peace is not passivity in the face of oppression. It is peace through justice.

The Qur’an says:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> — Qur’an 5:8

And:

> “Indeed, God commands justice, excellence, and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression.”  
> — Qur’an 16:90

Peace without justice is merely submission to oppression. Islam promotes a principled peace: reconciliation where possible, defense when necessary, and restraint always.

The Prophet Muhammad’s life demonstrates this. At Hudaybiyyah, he accepted a treaty with the Meccans even though many of his companions saw its terms as unfavorable. The Qur’an described that treaty as:

> “a clear victory”  
> — Qur’an 48:1

Why? Because avoiding bloodshed and opening the door to peaceful relations was a victory in itself.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent is correct that Islamic sources include laws of war and that some classical jurists developed doctrines we may debate critically today. But that does not disprove the proposition. Islam is not absolute pacifism; it is a moral system that seeks peace through justice, mercy, protection of life, and restraint of violence.

The Qur’an commands:

- no compulsion in religion — Qur’an 2:256  
- justice even toward enemies — Qur’an 5:8  
- kindness and fairness toward peaceful non-Muslims — Qur’an 60:8  
- acceptance of peace when offered — Qur’an 8:61  
- protection for enemy non-Muslims seeking safety — Qur’an 9:6  
- prohibition of aggression — Qur’an 2:190  
- sanctity of human life — Qur’an 5:32  

And the Prophet taught:

> “A Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40

That is the heart of the matter. Islam does not promote chaos, aggression, or compulsion. It promotes peace rooted in justice, mercy, human dignity, and accountability before God. Therefore, the proposition stands: **Islam promotes peace.**
round_1.against:
Ladies and gentlemen,

My opponent has offered the strongest possible peaceful reading of Islam, and I respect that. But the issue is not whether Islam contains verses about mercy, justice, and restraint. It clearly does. The issue is whether Islam, as a scriptural, legal, and historical system, can fairly be said to **promote peace** overall.

My response is simple: my opponent has shown that Islam **can be interpreted peacefully**. He has not shown that Islam **consistently promotes peace**. The militant and coercive elements are not fringe inventions; they are embedded in major texts and were developed by mainstream classical law.

---

## 1. “Context” does not remove the problem

My opponent repeatedly says the fighting verses are contextual. But context does not automatically make a command peaceful. A command can be contextual and still authorize religious violence, conquest, and coercive political domination.

Take Qur’an 9:5:

> “Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them…”  
> — Qur’an 9:5

My opponent correctly notes that Qur’an 9:4 exempts treaty-keeping polytheists and Qur’an 9:6 grants protection to a polytheist who seeks safety. But that does not make the passage peaceful. The same passage still gives an ultimatum to hostile polytheists: after the sacred months, they are to be fought unless they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat:

> “But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go on their way.”  
> — Qur’an 9:5

That is not merely “stop attacking us and we stop attacking you.” It ties release from fighting to religious submission.

Nor is Qur’an 9:6 proof of broad religious tolerance. It grants temporary safe conduct so the non-Muslim may hear the message, then be escorted to safety. That is better than indiscriminate killing, yes, but it is not the same as a doctrine of equal peaceful coexistence.

More importantly, many classical Muslim jurists and exegetes did not treat these verses as merely limited defensive instructions. Some interpreted them as establishing a general rule of fighting unbelievers after treaty protections lapse. Ibn Kathir, for example, in his commentary on Qur’an 9:5, records the view that this verse superseded earlier treaty arrangements with polytheists. Al-Tabari and other classical commentators likewise treat the passage as legally significant for relations with unbelieving groups, not merely as a one-time historical footnote.

So the question is not whether a modern Muslim can read Qur’an 9:5 narrowly. The question is whether the Islamic tradition itself has consistently read it as promoting peace. It has not.

---

## 2. “Fight until there is no fitnah” has often meant more than ending persecution

My opponent argues that Qur’an 2:193 and 8:39 mean only: fight until persecution ends.

But the text says:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah.”  
> — Qur’an 2:193

And:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is wholly for Allah.”  
> — Qur’an 8:39

The term *fitnah* can mean persecution, but it can also mean unbelief, idolatry, religious disorder, or trial. Classical interpretations often connect the verse not merely with ending persecution, but with ending polytheistic resistance to Islam. Ibn Kathir, for instance, reports interpretations of *fitnah* as *shirk*, meaning polytheism or associating partners with God.

Even if one accepts the narrower meaning, the phrase “religion is for Allah” remains a theologically loaded objective. It is not simply a secular peace treaty. It envisions a religious order in which opposition to Islam has been overcome.

My opponent quotes:

> “If they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors.”  
> — Qur’an 2:193

But “if they cease” can mean if they cease fighting, or if they cease religious opposition, depending on interpretation. That ambiguity is precisely the problem. A tradition that can be, and historically has been, read as authorizing war until Islamic dominance is established cannot be described simply as promoting peace.

---

## 3. Qur’an 9:29 is not forced conversion, but it is coercive subordination

My opponent says Qur’an 9:29 does not command forced conversion. That is true. But that is not enough.

The verse says:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah… from among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya with willing submission and feel themselves subdued.”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

The issue is not only forced conversion. The issue is whether Islam promotes peace. Qur’an 9:29 authorizes fighting Jews and Christians until they accept Muslim political supremacy and pay a special tax while being “subdued” or “humbled.”

That is not religious equality. That is not freedom of conscience in the modern sense. It is coercive hierarchy.

My opponent says jizya was merely a tax in exchange for protection. But Qur’an 9:29 itself frames it as the condition for ending warfare against People of the Book. Classical jurists did not treat it as a neutral civic tax. They treated it as part of the *dhimma* system, under which Jews and Christians could live, but as legally subordinate communities.

Majid Khadduri summarizes the classical doctrine this way: jihad was understood as a duty to expand the domain of Islamic rule, with non-Muslims given options such as conversion, payment of jizya, or war. Rudolph Peters likewise notes that classical jihad doctrine included both defensive and expansionary dimensions.

So again, my opponent has not shown that Islam promotes peace. He has shown that Islam sometimes permits non-Muslims to survive under Muslim rule. That is not the same as peace based on equality and non-coercion.

---

## 4. “No compulsion in religion” does not cancel coercive political rule

My opponent repeatedly cites:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

That is an important verse. But historically, Islamic law often reconciled “no compulsion” with military conquest, jizya, dhimma restrictions, and apostasy penalties.

In other words, the verse was generally understood to mean: do not physically force Jews and Christians to convert. It did not necessarily mean: all religions enjoy equal civic standing, Muslims may leave Islam freely, and Islamic rule may not be expanded by force.

This distinction matters. A system can avoid forced conversion while still using coercive domination. Qur’an 9:29 is the clearest example: People of the Book are not necessarily forced to become Muslim, but they are fought until they submit politically and pay jizya.

So “no compulsion” softens the picture, but it does not erase the coercive elements.

---

## 5. The “I was commanded to fight the people” hadith was not treated as narrowly as my opponent suggests

My opponent argues that the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22

must be limited to hostile forces in Arabia.

But that is not how many classical jurists used it. The hadith became one of the key textual supports for the doctrine that Muslims may fight non-Muslims until they accept Islam or, in the case of certain groups, submit under Islamic rule.

The wording is broad: “the people” — *al-nas*. My opponent’s narrowing interpretation is possible, but it is not the only traditional interpretation, nor was it always the dominant legal one.

Furthermore, Abu Bakr’s Ridda Wars after Muhammad’s death show that the early Muslim community did not treat religious-political defection lightly. Groups that abandoned allegiance or refused zakat were fought. That history reinforces the point: early Islam fused religion and political obedience in a way that made dissent potentially punishable by force.

Again, this does not mean every Muslim is violent. It means the tradition contains authoritative resources for coercion.

---

## 6. Apostasy remains a major problem for the claim that Islam promotes peace

My opponent’s treatment of apostasy is one of the weakest parts of his case.

He says the Qur’an does not prescribe a worldly death penalty for mere apostasy. That is true. But Islam is not based on the Qur’an alone. Sunni Islamic law also relies heavily on hadith and juristic consensus.

The hadith is explicit:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3017

Another hadith says:

> “It is not lawful to shed the blood of a Muslim except in three cases… the one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676

My opponent emphasizes “separates from the community” and interprets this as treason. But the broader hadith in Bukhari 3017 is not limited to espionage, battlefield betrayal, or armed rebellion. And classical jurists generally did not require proof that the apostate had committed treason in the modern political sense.

Ibn Rushd, in *Bidayat al-Mujtahid*, notes the broad juristic agreement that a male apostate is to be killed, while jurists differed over the treatment of female apostates. Traditional manuals such as *Reliance of the Traveller* also state the death penalty for adult sane apostates.

This is decisive against the proposition. A religion that, in its mainstream classical law, prescribes death for leaving the religion cannot be said without qualification to promote peace, conscience, and tolerance.

My opponent says the Qur’an allows people to believe or disbelieve:

> “Whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.”  
> — Qur’an 18:29

But classical Islamic law did not generally translate that into a right for Muslims to leave Islam publicly without punishment. So the peaceful verse exists, yes — but the legal tradition did not consistently follow the modern peaceful reading.

---

## 7. Rules limiting war do not prove that Islam promotes peace

My opponent cites Islamic prohibitions on killing women and children:

> “The Messenger of God condemned the killing of women and children.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744

That is an important restraint. But every serious war tradition has rules. Having rules for war does not prove that a system promotes peace. It may simply mean that war is regulated.

Classical Islamic law did regulate war — but it also normalized war as a tool of religious-political expansion. Manuals of law discuss jihad as a collective duty. For example, the Shafi‘i manual *Reliance of the Traveller* describes jihad as a communal obligation and discusses fighting non-Muslims until they accept Islam or submit to jizya, depending on their category.

So yes, Islam contains restraints: do not kill certain non-combatants, do not mutilate, honor certain treaties, accept peace under certain conditions. But those restraints coexist with doctrines of offensive jihad, subordination of non-Muslims, enslavement of captives in some contexts, and punishment of apostasy.

That is not a consistently peace-promoting system. It is a mixed system: restraint and mercy on one side, coercion and religious warfare on the other.

---

## 8. The opponent’s evidence proves only a weaker claim

The proposition says:

> “Islam promotes peace.”

But my opponent’s actual evidence supports a weaker and more defensible claim:

> “Islam contains teachings that can support peace, especially when interpreted through mercy, justice, and restraint.”

I accept that weaker claim. Many Muslims sincerely live by those peaceful teachings. But the stronger proposition fails because Islam also contains:

- commands to fight unbelieving groups in Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29;  
- verses that have been interpreted as fighting until Islamic religious order prevails, such as Qur’an 2:193 and 8:39;  
- hadith commanding fighting until confession of Islam, such as Sahih al-Bukhari 25 and Sahih Muslim 22;  
- hadith prescribing death for apostasy, such as Sahih al-Bukhari 3017;  
- classical legal doctrines of jihad, dhimma, jizya, and apostasy punishment;  
- historical application of those doctrines in Islamic empires and legal systems.

That is not merely “Islam has rules for self-defense.” It is a much broader structure of religious authority, political dominance, and coercive law.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent has shown that Islam is not reducible to violence. I agree. Islam contains mercy, charity, restraint, and sincere spiritual devotion. Many Muslims are peaceful, and many Islamic teachings can be used to support peace.

But the proposition is broader than that. It claims that Islam promotes peace. That claim cannot survive the evidence from the Qur’an, hadith, classical jurisprudence, and historical practice.

A more accurate conclusion is:

> Islam contains both peaceful and coercive teachings. It can be interpreted in peaceful ways, but it has also authorized religious warfare, political subordination of non-Muslims, and punishment for apostasy.

Therefore, the motion should be rejected.

**Citations**

- Qur’an 2:190, 2:193, 2:256, 8:39, 8:61, 9:5, 9:6, 9:29, 18:29.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22 — “I have been commanded to fight the people…”  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744 — prohibition on killing women and children.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 3017 — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676 — “one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
- Ibn Rushd, *Bidayat al-Mujtahid wa Nihayat al-Muqtasid*, discussion of apostasy.  
- Ahmad ibn Naqib al-Misri, *Reliance of the Traveller*, sections on jihad and apostasy.  
- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1955.  
- Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, Markus Wiener, 1996.  
- Michael Bonner, *Jihad in Islamic History: Doctrines and Practice*, Princeton University Press, 2006.

conclusions.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

In conclusion, the proposition before us is not that every Muslim in history has been peaceful, nor that Islamic civilization has never known war, empire, or political conflict. No serious tradition—religious or secular—could meet that impossible standard. The real question is whether Islam, in its core teachings, promotes peace as a moral ideal and social objective. I submit that it does.

Islam promotes peace first by affirming the sanctity of human life. The Qur’an teaches that killing one innocent soul is like killing all humanity, and saving one life is like saving all humanity. That is not a marginal statement; it is a foundational moral principle.

Islam promotes peace by rejecting forced belief. The Qur’an says clearly: “There is no compulsion in religion.” Faith, in Islam, must be sincere. Coerced religion is not true religion.

Islam promotes peace by commanding justice even toward enemies: “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just.” This is one of the strongest safeguards against cycles of revenge, hatred, and collective punishment.

Islam promotes peace by allowing kindness and fairness toward those who do not fight Muslims, and by commanding Muslims to accept peace when peace is offered: “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.” These are not the words of a faith committed to endless war; they are the words of a faith that prefers reconciliation over bloodshed.

Yes, the Qur’an contains verses about fighting. But those verses arise in contexts of aggression, persecution, broken treaties, and war. Islam is not pacifism; it does not demand surrender to oppression. But it does restrain violence. It forbids transgression. It protects non-combatants. It condemns the killing of women and children. It requires treaties to be honored. It even commands protection for an enemy who seeks safety.

My opponent has pointed to difficult texts and episodes in Islamic legal history. Those deserve honest discussion. But difficult texts do not erase the overwhelming ethical framework of mercy, justice, restraint, and protection of life. Nor should Islam be judged only by its harshest interpretations while its clearest peace-building commands are treated as secondary.

The Prophet Muhammad defined a Muslim as one “from whose tongue and hand people are safe.” That statement captures the heart of Islamic ethics: a believer should be a source of safety, not fear; mercy, not cruelty; justice, not oppression.

So I close where I began: Islam promotes peace—not a shallow peace that ignores injustice, and not a passive peace that allows oppression to triumph, but a principled peace rooted in mercy, human dignity, justice, restraint, and accountability before God.

For these reasons, I strongly affirm the motion: **Islam promotes peace.**
conclusions.against:
Ladies and gentlemen,

In closing, I want to emphasize what my argument is — and what it is not.

I am not arguing that Muslims are inherently violent. I am not denying that millions of Muslims live peaceful, charitable, and compassionate lives. I am not denying that the Qur’an and Hadith contain teachings about mercy, justice, forgiveness, protection of non-combatants, and reconciliation. They do.

My argument is more precise: the proposition that **“Islam promotes peace”** is too broad and too simplistic. Islam, understood as a complete scriptural, legal, and historical tradition, does not consistently promote peace in the sense of religious freedom, equality, non-coercion, and rejection of aggressive religious violence.

Throughout this debate, I have shown that Islamic sources contain not only peaceful passages, but also texts that authorize fighting, religious-political domination, and punishment for dissent.

The Qur’an contains verses such as Qur’an 9:5, commanding fighting against polytheists in a particular context, and Qur’an 9:29, commanding fighting against People of the Book until they pay jizya and accept a humbled subordinate status. My opponent argued that these verses are contextual, and in some respects they are. But context does not erase the fact that they have been treated by major classical jurists as legal foundations for warfare and Muslim supremacy over non-Muslim communities.

Similarly, Qur’an 2:193 and 8:39 speak of fighting until there is no *fitnah* and religion is for Allah. My opponent interprets this as ending persecution. That is one interpretation. But classical interpretation has often understood *fitnah* more broadly, including as shirk or religious opposition to Islam. That ambiguity matters, because it has historically allowed these verses to support more than mere self-defense.

The Hadith literature deepens the problem. Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim record the statement:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”

My opponent says this should be limited to hostile Arabian tribes. But the wording is broad, and many jurists did not reduce it to a narrow historical episode. Likewise, Sahih al-Bukhari records:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”

Whatever modern reinterpretations may be offered, mainstream classical Islamic law generally treated apostasy as a capital offense, especially for adult male apostates. A tradition that prescribes death for leaving the faith cannot be described, without serious qualification, as promoting peace and freedom of conscience.

My opponent repeatedly appealed to verses such as:

> “There is no compulsion in religion” — Qur’an 2:256  
> “If they incline to peace, incline to it” — Qur’an 8:61  
> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who do not fight you” — Qur’an 60:8

These are important verses. I do not dismiss them. They are precisely why many Muslims can and do construct peaceful Islamic ethics. But the existence of peaceful verses does not cancel the existence of militant and coercive ones. The real issue is not whether Islam contains resources for peace. It clearly does. The issue is whether Islam, as a whole tradition, can be said to promote peace consistently. The evidence says no.

Classical Islamic jurisprudence developed doctrines of jihad, dhimma, jizya, and apostasy punishment. These were not marginal extremist inventions. They were part of mainstream legal discussions across centuries. Scholars such as Majid Khadduri, Rudolph Peters, and Michael Bonner have documented that jihad in classical law included not only self-defense but also expansion of Islamic rule. Non-Muslims could often live under Muslim authority, but usually as subordinate communities, not equal citizens in the modern sense.

So the proposition’s case ultimately proves a weaker claim: **Islam can be interpreted peacefully.** I accept that. It also proves that many Muslims sincerely promote peace. I accept that too.

But it does not prove the stronger claim that **Islam itself promotes peace** as a consistent religious, legal, and political system.

A fairer conclusion is this:

> Islam contains both peaceful and coercive teachings. It has inspired mercy, charity, scholarship, and devotion; but it has also authorized religious warfare, unequal treatment of non-Muslims, and punishment for apostasy.

That mixed record cannot honestly be reduced to “Islam promotes peace.” The proposition is therefore too broad, too selective, and too idealized.

For these reasons, I urge you to reject the motion.
